text:
The next morning I telephoned the hospital and said I was ill. It was not exactly a lie, because my hands would not stop trembling and my stomach felt like a fist.

The answer on the paper had been short. It said only, Don't go out tonight. I had never written those words, and the paper on my real door was still the old one, my own question, completely untouched.

I decided that if the camera showed tomorrow, then tomorrow could be changed. I simply would not be here. I pulled two suitcases from the bedroom closet and started packing the car.

I moved quickly, carrying clothing, medication, my laptop, and a framed photograph of my mother. I knocked my elbow against the counter while carrying the last box through the hallway. A water glass slid off the edge and burst across the kitchen tiles.

I knelt to gather the pieces, and a long fragment of glass went straight into the heel of my left hand. The blood came quickly, bright and warm. In the bathroom I washed the cut, closed it with adhesive strips, and wrapped it in white gauze, pinned at the end with two tiny metal clips. It took five minutes, and I did it perfectly, because I always do.

Hale watched from across the street as I shut the trunk, and when I waved with my good hand, he did not wave back.

I drove for an hour and stopped at a motel beside the highway, where I locked the door, closed the curtains, and sat on the bed with my phone. I told myself that distance would break the pattern, and that nobody could possibly find me there.

At 3:12 the phone chimed. I opened the recording with my thumb, and the hooded figure stood on my porch, facing the door, perfectly motionless. Its left hand hung at its side, wrapped in white gauze and pinned at the end with two tiny metal clips.
summary: She calls in sick and flees to a motel, cuts her left hand on broken glass and bandages it with white gauze, and the next recording shows the figure with the same bandage.
